meta: Robert Edge Pine's 1780 portrait of Patience Lovell Wright, the colonial sculptor who modelled famous people in tinted wax.
about: An elderly woman in a white bonnet and a draped white shawl over a rose-pink dress gazes upward against a dark ground. She is Patience Wright, born at Oyster Bay, New York, and one of the first professional sculptors of the colonial period. She modelled portraits of famous people in tinted wax. After her husband died in 1769 she took up the work to support her five children. She moved to England in 1772, where King George III was among her admirers, and she hosted pro-revolutionary meetings in her studio.

meta: Willem Joseph Laquy's 1770 triptych allegory of art training, with a birth room for nature and a night school for education.
about: Three panels make up an allegory of art education. In the middle a woman nurses a child in a birth room, with a cradle and a basket at her feet, a stuffed deer's head on the wall and a dentist at work behind. This room stands for nature. The left panel shows an evening school, where pupils learn to write by the light of candles and a lantern, and it stands for education. On the right panel a scholar trims a pen by candlelight in his study. The Rijksmuseum bought it with support from the Vereniging Rembrandt.

meta: William Alfred Delamotte's 1830 watercolour of the drawing room at Middleton Park, Oxfordshire, a mix of Chinese motifs and Regency furniture.
about: Flamboyant Chinese motifs share this room with plain English Regency chairs and cases. Bamboo appears in more furniture, in door and shutter panels and in the fretwork frame of the mirror over the fireplace. The ceiling frieze is painted blue with gold Chinese characters, and a birdcage hangs from it, which suits the Chinese wallpaper and porcelains. Books and baskets lie scattered on the floor. Flowers and plants fill the room in true Victorian style, and the drapery is elaborate for the period.

meta: Emilio Sala's 1878 portrait of the girl María Guerrero, bought for the Prado's predecessor museum in 1955.
about: A young girl with dark hair sits on a bentwood chair in a light room, her chin resting on one hand. She wears a blue dress with white trim and white socks. Emilio Sala painted her in loose, visible brushwork. The Spanish state bought the painting from María Fernanda Ladrón de Guevara by ministerial order of 28 December 1955. It was meant for the former Museo de Arte Moderno in Madrid.

meta: Emmanuel Tzanes's 1644 icon The Vine of the Virgin, a Tree of Jesse in the Late Cretan tradition.
about: A standing woman in a red mantle and dark robe is rooted in a family tree of her ancestors. Emmanuel Tzanes made this tempera icon in 1644. Wikipedia describes him as one of the most prolific Greek painters of the seventeenth century, with more than 130 known works. He was active in Crete, Corfu and Venice, where he settled and served as a priest at San Giorgio dei Greci. Flemish engravings strongly influenced Greek painters in the Venetian lands by then. The Tree of Jesse shows the ancestors of Jesus Christ and the Virgin Mary, and it comes from a passage in the Book of Isaiah.

meta: Hans Eworth's 1554 portrait of Mary I of England, at the Society of Antiquaries of London.
about: A woman stands full length before a red damask hanging in a gold brocade gown with jeweled sleeves and a dark fur-trimmed cloak. Her hands are held together at the waist and wear rings. She is Mary I of England. The painting is signed HF 1554, but the first initial was originally an E, for Hans Eworth. It is oil on an oak panel more than a metre high and belongs to the Society of Antiquaries of London.

meta: John Steuart Curry's 1929 Tornado over Kansas, a farm family running for shelter that Kansans disliked.
about: A funnel cloud rises over a flat prairie beneath a bruised green and violet sky while a farm family hurries toward shelter. John Steuart Curry painted it in 1929. Wikipedia says he feared natural disasters from childhood, and that fear shows in the picture. It first appeared in 1930 and was thought a notable Regionalist work, but native Kansans disliked its subject. Fellow painters Stuart Davis and Thomas Hart Benton criticized Curry's amateur style. It has hung in the Muskegon Museum of Art since 1935.

meta: William Collins's 1814 portrait of Ferdinand VII of Spain, given to the Prado in 1889 by the Duchess of Pastrana.
about: A man stands in a dark coat with red facings, silver lace trim and a light blue sash, a gold decoration on his chest. He rests his hand on a map. A gold-trimmed crimson crown and yellow drapery appear at the left. The sitter is Ferdinand VII of Spain. The Duchess of Pastrana, María Dionisia Vives y Zires, gave the portrait to the museum in 1889. It was in the Museo de Arte Moderno from 1896 to 1971.

meta: Joshua Johnson's portrait Mr. Baylor, painted around 1805, which descended in the sitter's family before the Garbisches bought it in 1956.
about: A man with reddish hair and a slight smile sits in a yellow wooden chair against a muted olive ground. He wears a dark coat and a white cravat, and he holds a quill pen and a folded sheet of handwritten paper. Joshua Johnson painted him around 1805. The portrait went down in the sitter's family to a Mrs. Baylor of Hagerstown, Maryland. In 1956 a Baltimore dealer sold it to Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch, and it was given to the National Gallery of Art in 1978.
credit_line: Gift of Edgar William and Bernice Chrysler Garbisch

meta: A 1610 drawing of the Assumption of the Virgin once given to Ventura Salimbeni, an attribution now doubted.
about: The Virgin reclines on clouds in a glory of rays, her arms outstretched. At the left an angel plays the lute and at the right another plays the organ, each with a group of angels. Cherubim crowd below. The sheet is in pen and brown ink with brown wash. A note records that Philip Pouncy, in 1958, spoke against the attribution to Ventura Salimbeni. The museum also points to a related drawing in a 1928 Augsburg collection catalogue.

meta: Anson Dickinson's miniature of John Gadsby Jr., painted in Washington as a stickpin.
about: A man with curly dark hair and blue eyes wears a dark coat over a white cravat, in an oval miniature set in a gilt frame. It was originally a stickpin, mounted on a long pin that was pushed through the wearer's cravat. Anson Dickinson painted it in Washington, D.C., where he was based at the time. The sitter, John Gadsby Jr., was the son of the tavern keeper John Gadsby, owner of Gadsby's Tavern in Alexandria, Virginia. That tavern hosted Thomas Jefferson's inaugural dinner.

meta: Eelke Jelles Eelkema's 1815 still life of flowers on a stone plinth, given to the Rijksmuseum in 1942.
about: A bouquet of roses, tulips, narcissi and irises stands on a stone plinth. Pinks and cuckoo flowers join them, and a few butterflies hover among the blooms. A book lies at the right. Eelke Jelles Eelkema signed the painting at lower left. Mrs J.J. Kramer and Mrs E.S. Kramer of The Hague gave it to the Rijksmuseum in 1942, together with other objects.

meta: Gerrit Lundens's 1642 copy of Rembrandt's Night Watch, which shows parts of the original that were later cut away.
about: A dimly lit group of militiamen with muskets gathers under a dark stone archway. A blue and gold banner rises at the left and a drummer stands at the right. Captain Banning Cocq is in the centre in black with a red sash. Gerrit Lundens made this copy of Rembrandt's Night Watch. Wikimedia Commons calls it particularly important because it shows sections of the original that were cut away and lost in the 18th century. It is in the National Gallery in London.

meta: Sarah Goodridge's 1820 portrait of Chief Justice Theophilus Parsons, a Massachusetts lawyer.
about: A man with tousled brown hair wears a dark coat and white cravat against a plain grey ground, in an ornate gilt frame. He is Theophilus Parsons, a leading lawyer in New England. Parsons wrote the Essex Report, which set out many principles of republican government, and he helped draft the Massachusetts constitution. He served as chief justice of the state's Supreme Judicial Court from 1806 to 1813. The museum calls him somewhat eccentric. His wife often went with him to make sure he looked presentable.

meta: Watanabe Shiko's six-panel screen of flowers and trees of the four seasons, painted with gold and silver.
about: Flowering plants with broad green leaves, and a tree with white and green foliage, stand against a gold leaf ground with stylized clouds. Watanabe Shiko had a special interest in scientific realism, which grew out of his contacts with his patron Konoe Iehiro. He combined accurate plant drawing with strong ink outlines and decorative gold and silver. The Cleveland Museum of Art says this produced an innovative style that influenced many of his peers in Kyoto. One plant in the screens is turmeric, which grows in Okinawa.
credit_line: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

meta: Tanzio da Varallo's Portrait of a Man, painted around 1620, with a carefully drawn rapier of North Italian make.
about: A man in a dark doublet with white lace collar and cuffs wears a red sash and a gold-hilted sword. He holds a baton in one hand and a plumed red hat in the other. His name is unknown. The museum notes that the sword is a rapier, a blade worn with civilian dress and used in duels. By its style the hilt belongs to a group decorated between about 1570 and 1600, and it was probably made in northern Italy.

meta: Bastiaan de Poorter's 1852 posthumous portrait of Hendrik André Cornelis Tierens, a city official of Heusden.
about: A man with grey curly hair, a dark coat and a white cravat is shown to the waist in an oval, turned to the right against a deep red ground. He is Hendrik André Cornelis Tierens, a city functionary of Heusden who died in 1851. Bastiaan de Poorter painted him after his death and signed the picture. It has a pendant in the Rijksmuseum.

meta: Francesco del Cossa's Crucifixion, painted around 1473 for Floriano Griffoni's family chapel in San Petronio, Bologna.
about: The crucified Christ hangs at the centre of a circular panel, with INRI on the titulus above him. A grieving woman in a dark hooded mantle stands to one side and a young man in a red cloak to the other. A skull lies at the foot of the cross. Floriano Griffoni commissioned it around 1473 for his family chapel in San Petronio in Bologna, and Vasari mentions it. It was moved to the Casa Aldrovandi about 1731 and had gone by 1782. Philip Lehman owned it by 1914.
dimensions:
overall (diameter of painted surface): 60 × 63.2 cm (23 5/8 × 24 7/8 in.)
framed: 103.51 × 102.87 × 18.42 cm (40 3/4 × 40 1/2 × 7 1/4 in.)

meta: Évariste-Vital Luminais's 1865 painting of a fisherman's family, bought from the artist for the museum in Blois.
about: Women and a young girl stand on a rocky coastal ledge above a wide, pale tidal flat with shallow pools. Two women in green and red skirts embrace, and one bows her head in grief. The title gives the subject as The Widow or the Fisherman's Family. The French state bought the picture from the artist in 1865 for the museum in the château at Blois. It stayed there until 1986. Then it went to the Louvre, which assigned it to the Musée d'Orsay.

meta: Alvan Fisher's 1820 view of the Horseshoe Fall at Niagara, one of two Niagara scenes by him.
about: The white curtain of water at the Horseshoe Fall pours over a curved edge beneath heavy clouds and a double rainbow. Small groups of people stand on the foreground ledge. Alvan Fisher painted two scenes of Niagara Falls, this one and A General View of the Falls of Niagara. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says they capture the thrill of visiting the falls, a site in upstate New York that quickly became a symbol of the continent's vast scale. Nothing here is small.

meta: Nathaniel Jocelyn's 1830 portrait of the abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison.
about: A man in a dark coat and black cravat wears wire-rimmed spectacles against a warm brown ground. He gazes straight at the viewer. He is William Lloyd Garrison, a printer and editor from Newburyport, Massachusetts. Around 1828 he converted to abolitionism, and in 1833 he founded the American Anti-Slavery Society. The National Portrait Gallery says he helped turn the antislavery movement from talk of gradual ending into a moral crusade for immediate emancipation. He was once nearly lynched in Boston.

meta: Kano Naonobu's six-panel screen of summer and winter landscapes, one of a pair that was once damaged and later conserved.
about: This sparse composition shows summer on the right and winter on the left. Snow-covered mountains, pines and thatched buildings stand beside a frozen field, with gold-flecked clouds above. Careful observation reveals that the pair of screens was once damaged. A later conservation added new sections of paper and inpainting, so the paintings could still be enjoyed with something of their original flavor. Kano Naonobu was born in Kyoto. He was the younger brother of the painter Kano Tan'yu, and in 1630 he moved to Edo at the request of the Tokugawa government.
credit_line: Gift from the Collection of George Gund III
